items.title: Bernard Purdie interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003
items.q: Now Gene Krupa helped us. Gene Krupa was one of the first persons to bring us out front so people could see the drums. So I always felt that way because that’s how I was taught when I was coming along.

ctx.x: Which usually came later? Or were they—

Oh no. This was all done at the same time. This was all done because we’re now dealing with two and four track. Two track and four track. But that’s — you know you’re dealing with the early stages, the stuff that none of the young people today would know or understand because they didn’t have to do it that way. They’ve never known anything like that. So going that way, what happened is that something happened within the rhythm section or a sound happened while you were in there. Now remember now, you already have…

you’ve got this rhythm section going and you start to create this sound. Something happens. Now you’ve got these three guitars. One is playing the backbeat (scats) and you’ve got rhythm (scats) and then you’ve got the other one might be a twang, it might be a thing with Vinnie Bell sound, water sound or a fish or a tree, a whistle. He had all kinds of little sound effects that he did. And this started to become part of the sound to go with the hook of what is happening, the thing that’s going to be repeated over…
